When to reach for contrast

The 2018 ASE guideline update recommends an ultrasound enhancing agent in these situations.

Rest

Two or more left ventricular segments are not seen well enough to assess function or wall motion.

Class I · LOE A
Stress

Any segment in a coronary territory cannot be adequately seen without contrast.

Class I · LOE A
Ejection fraction

An accurate LVEF will affect prognosis or management.

Class I · LOE B-R
LV thrombus

A thrombus cannot be confidently ruled in or out on non-contrast echo.

Class I · LOE B-NR

Source: Clinical Applications of Ultrasonic Enhancing Agents in Echocardiography: 2018 ASE Guidelines Update, J Am Soc Echocardiogr, March 2018. Guideline recommendations apply to ultrasound enhancing agents as a class.

Safety in practice

The questions that come up in the lab, answered plainly. Full details are in the prescribing information and boxed warning.

Before
  • Screen for known or suspected hypersensitivity to the microspheres or their components, including polyethylene glycol (PEG). Lumason is contraindicated in these patients.
  • Ask about prior reactions to PEG-containing products.
  • Note any cardiac shunt: the label warns of systemic embolization in patients with cardiac shunts.
During
  • Have resuscitation equipment and trained personnel readily available.
  • Keep the mechanical index at or below 0.8.
After
  • Observe the patient: most serious cardiopulmonary reactions occur within 30 minutes of administration.
  • Report adverse events to Bracco Drug Safety (1-800-257-5181, option 1) or FDA MedWatch.

Critically ill patients

The 2018 ASE update notes that large propensity-matched studies found no increase in mortality with ultrasound enhancing agents in critically ill patients.

Source: 2018 ASE Guidelines Update.

Patients with PEG hypersensitivity

Lumason contains PEG and should not be used in these patients. A clear plan for them belongs in every lab protocol.

Bracco medical to advise on how this is addressed.

Echo lab protocol card

Everything a sonographer needs at the bedside, on one printable card.

LUMASON® · Echocardiography quick referenceDemo draft · verify against current prescribing information
Adult dose

2 mL IV bolus. A second 2 mL bolus if needed.

Pediatric dose

0.03 mL/kg IV bolus, repeat once if needed. Do not exceed 2.0 mL per injection.

Flush

Follow each injection with 0.9% Sodium Chloride.

Preparation

Agitate in hand. No activation device. No refrigeration.

Mechanical index

Not recommended above 0.8. ASE recommends very-low-MI imaging for LV opacification.

Technique tip (ASE)

Small bolus with a slow saline flush helps limit apical shadowing.

Boxed warning

Serious cardiopulmonary reactions, including fatalities, have occurred. Most occur within 30 minutes. Have resuscitation equipment and trained personnel available.

Contraindication

Known or suspected hypersensitivity to the microspheres or their components, such as PEG.

Pediatric cardiology

Echo contrast for children, dosed by weight

Lumason is approved for pediatric patients with suboptimal echocardiograms, at 0.03 mL/kg, up to 2.0 mL per injection.

Many children with congenital heart disease have shunts. The label warns of systemic embolization in patients with cardiac shunts, so pediatric teams need clear guidance here.

The value for your echo lab

For echocardiography in the hospital outpatient setting, contrast payment is bundled with the echo. The 2026 Medicare increase applies to non-cardiac exams, not echo.

The value for cardiology is a study that answers the question the first time: fewer nondiagnostic echoes, fewer repeat or downstream tests, and a simpler workflow in the lab.

Bracco to supply approved data on nondiagnostic and downstream-test reduction.

Focal liver lesion characterization

Two studies compared three blinded readers with Lumason and with unenhanced ultrasound. Results as reported on lumason.com/liver.

Study A

MeasureWith LumasonUnenhanced
Sensitivity, malignant (N=119)76–92%16–49%
Specificity, benign (N=140)71–83%22–63%

Improvement significant for all readers except one specificity comparison (71% vs. 63%).

Study B

MeasureWith LumasonUnenhanced
Sensitivity, malignant (N=124)47–65%41–66%
Specificity, benign (N=116)67–88%7–59%

Specificity improved significantly for all three readers; sensitivity improved significantly for one reader and was lower for another.

Radiologists will read every row, so the full results belong here, including the mixed ones. Showing them builds trust.

Reading CEUS of the liver

Lumason shows dynamic lesion-to-liver enhancement through three phases, as described on lumason.com/liver.

Arterial

Early enhancement pattern of the lesion compared with surrounding liver.

Portal venous

Persistence or washout as the liver enhances.

Late

Sustained enhancement or washout helps separate benign from malignant patterns.

Bracco to supply: an annotated reading guide and pattern atlas, and confirm how ACR CEUS LI-RADS may be referenced.

Pediatrics

Imaging made for children: no radiation, and rarely any sedation*

Lumason is approved for children in three uses. It is the only US ultrasound contrast agent approved for pediatric liver imaging and for urinary tract reflux evaluation.

* For a contrast ultrasound of the urinary tract (ceVUS), sedation is rarely needed. Explaining the exam beforehand eases most children’s anxiety, and a parent or caregiver can stay close and help the child lie still. Each facility sets its own sedation practice. Source: RadiologyInfo.org, ceVUS.

◉Urinary tractVesicoureteral reflux, by intravesical use ◉LiverFocal liver lesion characterization ◉EchocardiographySuboptimal echocardiograms
No ionizing radiationUltrasound uses sound waves, not X-rays.
Sedation rarely neededUnlike MRI, which often requires sedation in infants and young children.
Parents and caregivers can stayA parent or caregiver can usually be beside the child during the exam.

Sources: RadiologyInfo.org; Laugesen et al., 2017.

Contrast-enhanced voiding urosonography

Lumason is approved for ultrasonography of the urinary tract to evaluate suspected or known vesicoureteral reflux in pediatric patients.

  • 1 mL Lumason given into the bladder through a catheter
  • The bladder may be refilled with saline for a second voiding cycle, without a second dose
  • No fluoroscopy, so no radiation, unlike a voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG)
  • Generally under 30 minutes

Effectiveness is based on two published studies in 411 pediatric patients.

Pediatric liver lesions

Lumason is the first and only ultrasound contrast agent approved to characterize focal liver lesions in children. A 2017 systematic review found CEUS performed comparably to CT and MRI for benign pediatric liver lesions, and can help reduce radiation exposure and iodinated contrast in children.

Laugesen et al., Ultrasound Int Open, 2017

Talking with families

What parents and caregivers ask, and honest answers to give.

Will my child need to be put to sleep?
Sedation is rarely needed for a contrast ultrasound.
Is there radiation?
No. Ultrasound uses sound waves.
Can I stay with my child?
Usually, yes. Parents and caregivers often help the child lie still.
Will it hurt?
An IV, or for a urinary tract exam a small bladder tube, can be uncomfortable. Most children manage well once it is explained.

Your child's exam

Here is what the day usually looks like.

  1. Before. Tell the care team about any allergies, including to polyethylene glycol (PEG), and about heart conditions. Little or no special preparation is usually needed.
  2. During. For a urinary tract exam, a nurse places a small soft tube in the bladder. It can feel uncomfortable, and the cleaning liquid may feel cold. The contrast goes in through the tube while the ultrasound takes pictures.
  3. You can help. You can usually stay right beside your child and help them lie still.
  4. After. Most children go back to their day. The whole exam usually takes less than 30 minutes.

Based on RadiologyInfo.org. Your care team will tell you what to expect for your child.

For your child

The bubble pictures

Bring along

  • A favorite toy, blanket or tablet
  • A list of your child's medicines and allergies
  • Your questions (see Questions to ask)

Your exam

  1. Before. Tell your care team about any allergies, including to polyethylene glycol (PEG), and about heart or lung conditions.
  2. During. The contrast is given through an IV in your arm, and the ultrasound happens as usual.
  3. After. Your care team will watch you for a short time afterward.

Why your doctor may have ordered it

To get a clearer view of your heart, or to learn more about a spot found in your liver on another scan, often without needing a different type of scan.

Why ultrasound

No radiationUltrasound uses sound waves.
No iodine or gadoliniumThe contrast is made of tiny gas-filled bubbles.
Usually no sedationSedation is rarely needed for a contrast ultrasound.
Close to youOften done in the ultrasound room or at the bedside.

Is it safe?

Like any medicine, contrast agents can cause side effects. Serious heart and lung reactions are uncommon but can happen, usually within 30 minutes, which is why your care team watches you closely and is ready to help.

The most common side effects are headache and nausea.

Do not have Lumason if you are allergic to it or to any of its ingredients, including polyethylene glycol (PEG).

Make your read, then see it with Lumason

81-year-old woman with coronary artery disease (after bypass surgery), type II diabetes and atrial fibrillation. Unenhanced apical four-chamber view.

What's your read on the apex?

How other readers answered (sample data for the demo)
Thrombus present
22%
No thrombus
19%
Can't tell
59%
Diagnosis: Thrombus ruled out in a patient with low ejection fraction. With Lumason, the left ventricle is dilated with severe segmental dysfunction and a dyskinetic septum; some apical motion is preserved, with no apical thrombus.

For PA-Cs, NPs and ordering clinicians

You order the echo or the liver study, and you are the one the patient asks, “Why do I need this?”

When contrast is worth requesting

  • The non-contrast echo may not answer the question, for example with body habitus, lung disease or a ventilated patient
  • An accurate ejection fraction will change management
  • A liver lesion is indeterminate on another scan
  • A child needs a urinary tract or liver evaluation without radiation

Flag before ordering

  • Known or suspected hypersensitivity to the microspheres or their components, such as PEG (contraindicated)
  • Cardiac shunts
Review flag: indications beyond the label (EF, ventilated patients) drawn from the 2018 ASE guideline update.

Your contrast ultrasoundWhat to expect

Your care team has ordered an ultrasound with a contrast agent called Lumason. It is made of tiny bubbles that help your care team see more clearly. There is no radiation.

Before

  • Tell your care team about any allergies, including to polyethylene glycol (PEG).
  • Tell them about any heart or lung conditions.

During

  • The contrast is given through an IV in your arm, and the ultrasound happens as usual.
  • For a child’s urinary tract exam, a nurse places a small soft tube in the bladder, and the contrast goes in through the tube. This can feel uncomfortable.

After

  • Your care team will watch you for a short time afterward.
  • Tell them right away if you feel unwell.

For children

  • Sedation is rarely needed.
  • A parent or caregiver can usually stay close.
  • Bring a favorite toy or blanket.

Questions? Ask your care team before the exam.

For nurses

You place the IV, prepare the room and watch the patient.

Before
  • Ask about allergies, including to PEG-containing products
  • Ask about heart conditions and known shunts
  • Confirm resuscitation equipment and trained personnel are available
During
  • IV bolus, followed by a 0.9% saline flush
After
  • Observe the patient: most serious reactions occur within 30 minutes
  • Report adverse events to Bracco Drug Safety (1-800-257-5181, option 1) or FDA MedWatch

Indications and Important Safety Information

Condensed for this demo. Final text must be Bracco's approved ISI.

WARNING: SERIOUS CARDIOPULMONARY REACTIONS

Serious cardiopulmonary reactions, including fatalities, have occurred uncommonly during or following the injection of ultrasound contrast agents, including sulfur hexafluoride lipid microspheres. Most serious reactions occur within 30 minutes of administration. Assess all patients for the presence of any condition that precludes administration. Always have resuscitation equipment and trained personnel readily available.

Indications

Echocardiography in adult and pediatric patients with suboptimal echocardiograms; characterization of focal liver lesions in adult and pediatric patients; and ultrasonography of the urinary tract for evaluation of suspected or known vesicoureteral reflux in pediatric patients.

Contraindications

Known or suspected hypersensitivity to sulfur hexafluoride lipid microspheres or their components, such as polyethylene glycol (PEG).

Warnings and precautions

Serious cardiopulmonary reactions; hypersensitivity reactions, including in patients with no prior exposure; systemic embolization in patients with cardiac shunts; ventricular arrhythmia at mechanical index above 0.8.

Adverse reactions

The most common adverse reactions are headache (1%) and nausea (0.5%). Report negative side effects to the FDA at fda.gov/medwatch or 1-800-FDA-1088.
